question: Which single check would have caught the attack earliest in the scenario?
options: Waiting for the HMI high-level alarm
A monthly review of historian trends
A monitoring rule on Modbus writes from hosts other than the HMI
Rebooting the HMI
explain: The write happened at minute 10 and produced a network event at once. The HMI alarm would never fire because the HMI showed replayed data, and monthly reviews are far too slow.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
question: What made the Unitronics compromises possible, according to CISA?
options: A zero-day in Modbus
Stolen certificates
Internet-facing PLCs with default or no passwords on default ports
Insider sabotage
explain: No advanced exploit was needed. Removing the devices from the internet and changing default passwords would have stopped this campaign; CISA's primary mitigations list exactly these.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
question: A company moves 30 apps behind one IdP. Which statement is true?
options: MFA and offboarding now happen in one place, and that place becomes the most valuable account system to attack
The apps can now verify Ana's MFA themselves
Each app no longer needs a session of its own
Password phishing becomes impossible
explain: Centralising login concentrates both benefit and risk: one place to enforce MFA and remove access, and one key that every app trusts. Apps still keep their own sessions, and the IdP's own login page can still be phished unless MFA is phishing-resistant.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
question: An SP checks the signature, Issuer and time window, but not the Audience. Which attack does that allow?
options: A malicious or compromised SP that receives the user's assertions can replay them to this SP and log in as those users
None, the signature is enough
XML signature wrapping
Login CSRF only
explain: Every SP that federates with the same IdP receives genuine, signed assertions about its users. Without the Audience check, any of them (or anyone who breaches one) can present those assertions here. It is the SAML twin of accepting a JWT with someone else's aud.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
question: An SP's library verifies a SAML signature using the certificate in the response's own KeyInfo element. What can an attacker do?
options: Sign an assertion with any key of their own and include its certificate, so verification succeeds
Nothing, the certificate proves who signed
Only replay old assertions
Only cause a denial of service
explain: A certificate in the message proves only that the message was signed with the key in that certificate. The trust decision must come from the IdP's metadata the SP stored in advance; Somorovsky's paper lists untrusted KeyInfo keys among the bugs it found.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: IdP compromise and Golden SAML: forging the whole federation
question: An attacker holds a stolen AD FS token-signing key. The security team resets every user's password and re-enrols MFA. What is the effect on forged assertions?
options: None: forged assertions never involve passwords or MFA, so they keep working until the key is replaced everywhere it is trusted
They stop working, because passwords changed
They work only for administrators
They work only until the next AD FS reboot
explain: Reiner's write-up and MITRE both make this point: forging bypasses authentication entirely. Only replacing the signing key (twice, lesson 14) and removing the attacker's access stop it.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
question: Which of these is an identity governance question rather than an authentication or per-request authorization question?
options: Did this login present a valid passkey for ana@corp.example?
Should Ana, who moved from finance to sales in March, still hold the payments role?
May the request GET /invoices/1002 return invoice 1002 to user 7?
Has this session cookie expired?
explain: Governance asks whether an entitlement should exist at all, over time. The passkey check and cookie expiry are authentication and session questions; the invoice check is the per-request authorization decision from the access control course.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Role mining and role engineering: from a pile of grants to roles
question: Why do role-mining tools use heuristics such as greedy selection instead of always finding the minimal set of roles?
options: Because minimal role sets are always insecure
Because Vaidya, Atluri and Guo showed the role mining problem is NP-complete, so exact solutions do not scale
Because RBAC forbids more than ten roles
Because the user-permission matrix is secret
explain: The 2007 SACMAT paper proved RMP NP-complete by reduction from the set basis problem. Large real matrices therefore need approximate methods.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Bastions, jump hosts and session brokering
question: Why is `ssh -J bastion db1` safer than logging in to the bastion and then running `ssh -A` onward?
options: Because -J uses a stronger cipher
Because with -J the end-to-end session runs from the laptop and keys stay there, while -A lets anyone who controls the bastion use the forwarded agent's keys
Because -J disables logging on the bastion
Because -A only works with passwords
explain: The ssh manual says agent forwarding lets users who can bypass file permissions on the remote host use the local agent, and names a jump host (-J) as the safer alternative.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Measuring identity hygiene, detecting abuse, and running the programme
question: A dashboard shows a median time to deprovision of 5 hours. Why is that not enough to call leaver handling healthy?
options: Because medians are always wrong
Because the median hides the tail: a few leavers keeping access for days, often through applications without connectors, is where incidents like Cash App's come from
Because 5 hours is longer than NIST allows
Because time to deprovision should be measured in days
explain: In the sample, the median is 5 hours but 4 of 12 leavers kept access for over a day and one for 400 hours. Report high percentiles and the maximum, and fix the systems that cause the tail.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: If every pixel value in D were doubled (D' = 2D), how would Otsu's threshold and mask change?
options: The threshold doubles and the mask stays the same
The threshold stays the same and the mask doubles in size
Both stay the same
The threshold quadruples because variance scales with the square
explain: Scaling all values by 2 multiplies every class mean by 2 and every variance by 4, so the ranking of splits is unchanged: the same pixels are separated, at a threshold value twice as large. The variance scales by 4, but the threshold is a pixel value, not a variance.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
question: Why should the incident bridge for a suspected intrusion run on an out-of-band channel?
options: Because corporate chat is too slow
Because regulators require it
Because the usual channels may be down, and an intruder with access may be reading them
Because out-of-band channels are encrypted and corporate ones are not
explain: Both reasons appear in real cases: the HSE lost email and phones, and CISA warned SolarWinds victims that the actor may watch defenders' activity, so remediation plans should be shared out of band.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
question: Six months later, a lawyer asks you to prove the memory image used in your report is the one taken from WKS-07. What answers that?
options: The custody log: who acquired it and when, each transfer, and the SHA-256 recorded at acquisition matching the image's hash today
The file name contains WKS-07
The file's modification date
Your memory of the day
explain: Names and dates are easy to change. A hash recorded at acquisition, matched today, plus an unbroken record of who held it, is the standard RFC 3227 and NIST describe.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
question: A process appears in windows.psscan output but not in windows.pslist. What is the right next step?
options: Investigate it: it may have exited, or it may have been unlinked from the active list to hide. Check its parent, times and command line
Ignore it; psscan produces false positives
Delete it from memory
Re-acquire memory because the image is corrupt
explain: psscan finds process structures anywhere in the image, including exited or hidden ones. A mismatch is not proof of malice, but it is exactly the kind of difference worth explaining.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
question: A listed US company determines on a Thursday that an incident is material. With no holidays, what is the latest day to file the Item 1.05 Form 8-K?
options: The following Monday
The following Tuesday
The following Wednesday
Exactly 96 hours later, on Monday
explain: The rule counts four business days after the determination: Friday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Weekends are skipped, so it is not a 96-hour calendar clock like GDPR's 72 hours.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL from zero: tables, queries, quotes and comments
question: What does `SELECT 'O''Brien';` return?
options: A syntax error, because there are three quotes
The text O'Brien
The text O''Brien with two quotes
The text O, then a second statement Brien
explain: Inside a string literal, two single quotes in a row stand for one quote character. The literal is 'O''Brien' and its value is O'Brien. A lone quote in the same place would end the literal instead.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
question: A developer escapes quotes in every input before building SQL. Which query is still injectable?
options: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<escaped input>'
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = <escaped input>
Neither; escaping quotes fixes SQL injection
Both, because escaping never works
explain: In the numeric query the input is not inside quotes, so there is nothing for quote escaping to do, and input such as 5 OR 1=1 changes the logic. The string query is protected by correct escaping in this dialect, which is exactly the fragile kind of guarantee to avoid.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: NoSQL injection: when a value turns into an operator
question: Why does a JSON body `{"password": {"$ne": ""}}` bypass a MongoDB login that uses `findOne({username, password})`?
options: MongoDB parses the password string as SQL
The value is an object, so MongoDB treats $ne as an operator and matches any non-empty password
The $ character disables authentication
MongoDB ignores fields it does not recognise
explain: No string was parsed. JSON allowed the client to send an object where the code expected a string, and objects with $ keys are operators in MongoDB queries.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: LDAP, XPath, header and log injection
question: An app checks logins with the LDAP filter `(&(uid=` + user + `)(userPassword=` + pw + `))`. Which defence does OWASP list first?
options: Parameterised LDAP queries, which every LDAP library provides
Escaping each value with an LDAP encoding function for the correct context (search filter or distinguished name)
Removing the letter u from input
Using HTTPS between the browser and the app
explain: LDAP APIs generally lack parameterised queries, so OWASP's first defence is escaping each variable with the correct library encoder: RFC 4515 rules for filters and RFC 4514 rules for distinguished names. Least privilege and allowlist validation come next.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
question: A hand-written submit path does: `*sq_tail = tail + 1;` then fills `sqe->fd`, `sqe->addr` and `sqe->len`, then calls `io_uring_enter`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since io_uring_enter is what actually submits
The tail must be decremented, not incremented
The kernel may read the SQE as soon as the tail moves (an SQPOLL thread can do so at any moment), so it can see stale fields; fill first, then release-store the tail
user_data must be set before fd
explain: The tail is the publication point. Once it moves, the SQE belongs to the kernel, and with SQPOLL a kernel thread may consume it without waiting for any system call. Always fill the SQE completely and then advance the tail with release semantics.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototypes: where a missing property comes from
question: Which statement about `JSON.parse('{"__proto__": {"x": 1}}')` is correct?
options: It immediately sets Object.prototype.x to 1
It throws, because __proto__ is a reserved key in JSON
It returns an object whose prototype is { x: 1 }
It returns an object with an own property named __proto__; no prototype changes until code copies that key elsewhere
explain: JSON.parse defines keys as own data properties, so __proto__ is just a name there (Object.keys shows it). Danger starts when later code assigns that key onto another object, for example in a merge or Object.assign, because assignment triggers the __proto__ setter.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: ReDoS: a regular expression that blocks every user
question: Cloudflare's postmortem compares `.*.*=.*;` with its lazy form `.*?.*?=.*?;` on the input x= followed by 20 x's. What did it find?
options: The lazy form needed 11 steps instead of 5,353
Both needed 5,353 steps: laziness changes the order of the search, not its size, when the match fails
The lazy form could not be compiled by PCRE
The greedy form failed while the lazy form matched
explain: Graham-Cumming showed that the lazy version of the semicolon pattern still took 5,353 steps for x= plus 20 x's, the same as the greedy one. Laziness only helped the pattern without the trailing semicolon, where a match exists early.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Deserialisation in JavaScript: node-serialize to React2Shell
question: Why does the React fix (`hasOwnProperty.call(moduleExports, name)`) stop the attack even though the payload format did not change?
options: It encrypts the Flight payload
It makes the decoder ignore names that are only reachable through the prototype chain, such as constructor and __proto__, so references cannot climb to Function
It blocks requests that contain the word constructor
It disables Server Functions entirely
explain: The vulnerability was an inherited lookup with an attacker-chosen name. Restricting lookups to own properties is the same gadget-side fix as lesson 6's Object.hasOwn. Keyword filters would be the fragile alternative the React team did not use.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Electron: when XSS in a desktop app becomes code execution
question: An Electron app keeps `nodeIntegration: false` but sets `contextIsolation: false` so its preload can share variables with the page. Why is that dangerous?
options: It is not: with nodeIntegration off, the page has no access to Node.js
It makes the app ignore its Content Security Policy
It disables HTTPS for remote content
The page shares built-ins with the preload, so injected script can replace methods such as Array.prototype.join that privileged preload code later calls
explain: This is the first bug in the Discord chain. Without isolation, preload and page share one JavaScript world, so XSS can tamper with built-ins used by code that has Node.js access. Electron's guide says contextIsolation is needed even when nodeIntegration is false.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: jemalloc: arenas, tcache, bitmap slabs and decay purging
question: Thread A allocates objects that thread B frees, and the two are bound to different arenas. Where does contention appear?
options: Nowhere, because each thread only ever touches its own arena
On every free, because B must lock A's arena per object
When B's tcache flushes: the batch is grouped by owning arena and B takes A's bin lock, the same lock A takes to refill
Only in the kernel, when pages are purged
explain: free goes into B's own tcache without a lock, so the per-call cost is low. But the bits live in A's slabs, so the flush must lock A's bin. Batching amortizes that, yet the lock is shared between the producer's refills and the consumer's flushes.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Histories: invoke, ok, fail, and the indeterminate info
question: Which completion in a client is a bug?
options: A read that timed out is recorded as fail
A write whose commit request was sent but whose socket then closed is recorded as fail
A cas that got etcd's key-not-found error is recorded as fail
A write that threw an unexpected exception is recorded as info
explain: Once the request has been sent, the database may have applied it, so the outcome is unknown and must be info. The read case is safe because reads have no effect, the key-not-found error proves the cas did not apply, and exceptions becoming info is Jepsen's default.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
question: A snapshot-isolated database is tested with Elle and the report shows only G2 cycles with two or more rw edges, no G-single, no G1. What should you conclude?
options: The database violates snapshot isolation
The history is consistent with snapshot isolation, though not with serializability
Elle failed, because a real system always shows G0
Nothing, because Elle cannot classify cycles
explain: Snapshot isolation forbids G0, G1 and G-single and allows G2 cycles whose rw edges are adjacent, like write skew. If two rw edges were never adjacent (Elle calls this G-nonadjacent), SI would be violated. Only a claim of serializability makes adjacent-rw G2 a violation, and a clean run never proves SI holds in general.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Measuring, caching and promoting without regressions
question: A tuning job reports a config 3 percent faster than the champion, measured once each on a shared GPU where run-to-run noise is about 5 percent. What is the cheapest correct response?
options: Promote it: 3 percent exceeds the typical 1 percent reporting threshold
Discard it: any difference under 5 percent is meaningless by definition
Re-measure both interleaved with about 44 repeats each, then compare the interval against zero
Promote it but add a note that the measurement was noisy
explain: At cv = 5 percent, detecting a 3 percent difference at 95 percent significance and 80 percent power needs roughly 15.7 x (5/3)^2 = 44 repeats per config. A difference smaller than the noise is not meaningless, it is simply not yet measured; the fix is more repeats (or less noise), and the decision rule is the interval on the difference, not the point estimate.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
question: Why does each lcore get its own mempool cache instead of every core taking buffers straight from the pool's shared ring?
options: To avoid a compare-and-swap on a shared, contended structure for every buffer; the cache refills in bulk
Because the shared ring can only be used by one core
Because caches are stored in the NIC
To make buffers physically contiguous
explain: Every access to the shared ring is an atomic operation on a cache line that all cores fight over. A private cache turns that into a plain array access, touching the shared ring only once per bulk refill or flush.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
question: A training step uses `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_AUX_BIAS` instead of `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_BIAS`. Why?
options: AUX makes the forward GELU more accurate
AUX disables the bias for the backward pass
AUX is required for BF16 outputs
Backward needs the GELU input, and AUX writes it out in the same kernel instead of a separate pass
explain: GELU's derivative depends on its input. Without saving the pre-activation, backward would have to recompute it from the matmul. The AUX epilogue writes it as a side output while the tile is already on chip.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Temperature: amplifying the small probabilities
question: You distill a large image classifier into a very small student with 30 units per layer. Following Hinton et al.'s MNIST findings, which temperature range is the best starting point?
options: T = 1, since small students need sharp targets
T = 20 or more, to transfer every logit
Temperature has no effect on small students
An intermediate T around 2.5 to 4
explain: With 30 units per layer, temperatures of 2.5 to 4 worked significantly better than higher or lower ones. A tiny student cannot absorb all the teacher's knowledge; an intermediate T lets it ignore the very negative, noisy logits while still learning the runner-up structure.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: word-level and sequence-level
question: After "the", the teacher gives cat 0.61 and dog 0.30; the student gives cat 0.35 and dog 0.45. How hard does each method push the student's dog logit down (the gradient on that logit)?
options: Both by 0.45, since cat is the teacher's top word in both cases
Word-level KD by 0.45; Seq-KD by 0.15
Word-level KD by 0.15; Seq-KD by 0.45
Word-level KD not at all; Seq-KD by 0.45
explain: The gradient of a cross-entropy on a logit is the student's probability minus the target. Word-level KD's target for dog is the teacher's 0.30, so 0.45 - 0.30 = 0.15. Seq-KD's target is one-hot on cat, so dog's target is 0 and the push is the full 0.45.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
question: A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128, and stores its cache in FP8. How many bytes per token?
options: 163,840 bytes
81,920 bytes
655,360 bytes
40,960 bytes
explain: $2 \times 40 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1 = 81{,}920$ bytes. 163,840 forgets that FP8 is 1 byte, 655,360 uses 32 heads at 2 bytes, and 40,960 drops the factor of 2 for keys plus values.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: A chat service uses a pure 4096-token sliding window. After the conversation passes 4096 tokens, output turns to gibberish. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Make the window 8192 tokens
Quantize the window to 4 bits
Also keep the first few tokens as attention sinks
Recompute the whole window every step
explain: The collapse begins when the initial tokens leave the window, so the softmax loses its sink. Keeping 4 initial tokens restored Llama-2-13B from perplexity 5158 to 5.40 in StreamingLLM. A bigger window only delays the failure.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving
question: A deployment loads a 2 GB cached prefix at 25 GB/s (80 ms) and computes the new tokens in 10 ms over 40 layers. Using the simplified overlap model, what TTFT should layer-wise loading give?
options: About 90 ms, because overlap cannot help a load-bound case
About 80 ms: the load dominates and only one layer of compute (0.25 ms) is exposed
About 45 ms, because the two streams split the work
About 10 ms, because the load is hidden behind compute
explain: max(80, 10) + min(80, 10)/40 = 80 + 0.25 ms. All compute hides under the load, but the load itself cannot hide behind anything. Sequential would be 90 ms, so overlap saves the 10 ms of compute and no more.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Lamport clocks: a counter that respects happened-before
question: A node's Lamport counter is 7. It receives a message stamped 4. What timestamp does the receive event get (using t = max(t, t_msg) + 1)?
explain: max(7, 4) + 1 = 8. The receive must be later than both the node's previous event (7) and the send (4). Answer 5 would put the receive before the node's own earlier event, breaking IR1. Answer 12 adds instead of taking the max.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
question: In a ColBERT system, which computation runs once per (query, candidate document) pair at search time?
options: The BERT pass over the document
The BERT pass over the query
The MaxSim between the query matrix and the document matrix
Projecting document tokens to 128 dimensions
explain: Document encoding (including the projection) happens offline, and the query is encoded once per query. Only the MaxSim, a few small matrix products and max operations, runs per candidate. A cross-encoder instead runs the whole transformer per pair.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Searching millions of passages: candidates, centroids, PLAID
question: Why can PLAID compute the query-to-centroid score matrix once and reuse it for every candidate passage?
options: Because every passage stores a copy of the centroids
Because centroids are a fixed shared vocabulary: each passage token is just a centroid id, so its approximate score is a lookup into the same matrix
Because the query has only one vector
Because residuals are all zero after compression
explain: All passages draw their centroid ids from the same set C. Once $S_{c,q} = C\,Q^{T}$ is computed, approximating any passage's MaxSim is a gather and max over rows of that matrix, with no new dot products and no decompression.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum
question: A GSM8k Coconut model uses c = 2. In training stage 2, what does an example with 4 reasoning steps look like?
options: Question, <bot>, 2 thoughts, <eot>, steps 3 and 4, answer
Question, <bot>, 4 thoughts, <eot>, steps 3 and 4, answer
Question, <bot>, 4 thoughts, <eot>, answer only
Question, <bot>, 2 thoughts, <eot>, steps 2, 3 and 4, answer
explain: Stage k removes the first k steps and inserts k x c thoughts: 2 x 2 = 4 thoughts. Steps 3 and 4 remain in language and carry the loss, together with the answer.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
question: Leaf L1 in the example has 9 keys and errors from -1 to +1, while the other leaves have zero error. If you could afford one more leaf model, where should it go?
options: Split L0, because it has the fewest keys
Split L1, because it has the widest error window and covers the most keys
Add it on top as a stage-0 model, to improve routing accuracy
Nowhere: zero-error leaves prove the RMI is already optimal
explain: Lookups routed to L1 search 3 slots and everyone else searches 1. Splitting L1 into two narrower slices is where extra capacity reduces search work. This is the intuition behind adaptive designs like ALEX and the error-driven segmentation of the PGM-index.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
question: Query: auto repair. Document: fix my car engine. Why does BM25 give this document a score of exactly 0, no matter how k1 and b are tuned?
options: Because the document is too short for length normalization
Because the IDF of auto is negative
Because BM25 needs at least two matching terms
Because BM25 only sums over query terms present in the document, and none are
explain: BM25 is a sum over query terms that occur in the document. With zero overlapping terms the sum is empty, so tuning cannot help. Expansion is what creates overlap.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: Why ranking needs its own loss function
question: A teammate proposes training the ranker by computing NDCG@10 on each batch and backpropagating through it. What happens?
options: Training works but is slower, because NDCG is expensive to compute
The gradient of NDCG with respect to the scores is zero almost everywhere, so the weights barely change
It works only if the labels are binary
It overfits, because NDCG uses the labels directly
explain: NDCG changes only when two documents swap order. Small score changes leave the sort, and therefore NDCG, unchanged, so the gradient is 0 (and undefined at the swap points). That is why LTR methods use a smooth surrogate or hand-designed gradients.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART in practice: libraries, truncation and click bias
question: Your LightGBM ranker fails with an error about labels after you switch to a 0 to 10 relevance scale. What is the likely cause?
options: LambdaRank only supports binary labels
group sizes must be equal
label_gain was set to five values, and every label must be smaller than the number of label_gain entries
eval_at must include 10
explain: LightGBM looks up each label's gain in label_gain, so labels must be smaller than its length. The default list has 31 entries, but a custom five-entry list only supports labels 0 to 4.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The delta rule: overwrite instead of add
question: Which statement about DeltaNet's $\beta_t$ is correct?
options: It is a fixed hyperparameter shared by all tokens
It is a per-token learning rate in (0,1) for an online regression step
It decays all of memory uniformly at each step
It must equal the norm of the key
explain: $\beta_t=\sigma(W_\beta x_t)$ is computed from the token, and in the gradient-descent view it is the step size. Uniform decay of all memory is a different mechanism (the gate $\alpha_t$ in the next lesson).

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: What a fixed state cannot do: recall limits and state tracking
question: A head has a $64\times64$ state stored in 16-bit numbers. What is the most random 32-bit values it could possibly store, under any encoding?
explain: 64 x 64 = 4,096 numbers, times 16 bits = 65,536 bits, divided by 32 bits per value = 2,048. Its linear read-out gives only about 64 clean slots, far fewer.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Permission bits: rwx, octal, umask and the kernel's check
question: app.log has owner root, group adm and mode 640. Bob is a member of adm. Can Bob read it? Can Bob append to it?
options: Neither
Both, because Bob is in the group
Append yes, read no
Read yes, append no
explain: Bob is not the owner but is in group adm, so the group triplet r-- applies: 4 means read only. Writing (including appending) needs the w bit, which only the owner has.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Services, systemd and cron: what runs without anyone logged in
question: An intruder with root wants code to run again after every reboot. Which of these places would a defender check? Pick the most complete answer.
options: Only /etc/crontab
Only /usr/lib/systemd/system, since admins never change /etc
/etc/systemd/system units and drop-ins, timers, system and user crontabs
/proc, because services are listed there
explain: Services, drop-ins and timers in /etc/systemd/system, and every crontab (system files and per-user tables), are all standard autostart places (ATT&CK T1543.002, T1053.003, T1053.006). /proc shows only what is running now.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Reading Linux logs: journald, auth.log, failed logins and sudo
question: Your Debian 12 server has no /var/log/auth.log. What is the most likely explanation?
options: SSH logging is disabled by default
An attacker deleted it
auth.log was renamed to secure
rsyslog is no longer installed by default, so authentication messages are only in the systemd journal
explain: Debian 12 release notes: rsyslog is no longer installed by default. Messages go to the journal; read them with journalctl -u ssh. An attacker is possible, but check the simple explanation first. /var/log/secure is the Red Hat name.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: CIS Benchmarks: what one recommendation contains
question: Your company must show PCI DSS and NIST SP 800-53 evidence for 300 Ubuntu servers. Why is a mapped benchmark rule useful here?
options: One automated check of a setting produces evidence for every framework that maps to that rule
It removes the need for any auditor
PCI DSS requires the CIS Level 2 profile by name
Mapped rules are enforced by the kernel
explain: Mapped content lets one check serve several frameworks. Auditors still review the evidence, PCI DSS does not mandate a CIS profile by name, and nothing about mapping involves the kernel.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Kernel lockdown modes and sysctl baselines across a fleet
question: Your EDR's eBPF sensor stops working after a hardening change. Which change most likely caused it?
options: lockdown=integrity on the kernel command line
module.sig_enforce=1
lockdown=confidentiality on the kernel command line
kernel.kptr_restrict = 1
explain: Confidentiality mode also refuses kprobes (reason 23) and BPF reads of kernel memory (reason 24), which tracing-based sensors depend on. Integrity mode allows them; module signing affects only modules.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: eBPF: small verified programs that watch the kernel from inside
question: What does the eBPF verifier guarantee about a program?
options: That it is not malicious
That it is signed by the kernel vendor
That it only reads, never writes
That it will finish and only access memory it is allowed to, so it cannot crash or hang the kernel
explain: The documentation is explicit: the verifier is a safety tool, not a security tool. A program that safely reports every password typed would pass it. Who may load programs is controlled by CAP_BPF, root and unprivileged_bpf_disabled.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: Ebury, an SSH backdoor on 400,000 servers over 15 years
question: In the lab run, `dpkg --verify libkeyutils1` exited 0 while the loaded library belonged to no package. What does that teach?
options: dpkg is broken
The attack is impossible on Debian-based systems
Symbolic links are always safe
Checksum verification only covers files the package owns; an extra file plus a repointed link needs an ownership check of what is actually loaded
explain: dpkg --verify only checksums the contents of the package's regular files. The repointed link is a package file, but dpkg does not check link targets, and the added .2 file belongs to no package, so nothing is flagged. (rpm -V does report a changed link.) Asking which package owns the resolved target (dpkg -S, rpm -qf) exposes it.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Case: regreSSHion across a fleet, from advisory to verified fix
question: After patching openssh-server on a host, why restart sshd?
options: The package manager requires it to finish installing
Already-running sshd processes keep executing the old code until the service restarts
To regenerate host keys
To reset LoginGraceTime
explain: Replacing the file on disk does not change code already loaded in memory. needrestart or an explicit restart makes the fix real.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a relevance judging prompt
question: Which prompt feature gave the largest average improvement in Bing's TREC Robust experiments?
options: Asking for aspect scores (match to intent, trustworthiness) before the overall score
Including the TREC description field
Adding the role statement
Asking for five simulated judges
explain: Aspects added +0.21 kappa on average. The authors suggest the step-by-step structure, not the particular aspects, is what helps; Bing uses several aspects in production.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
question: Why is an open-ended task such as summarization harder to score than a classification task?
options: Summaries are longer, so metrics run slower
Many different outputs can be equally good, so there is no single correct answer to compare against
Classification has no notion of quality
Summaries cannot be read by humans reliably
explain: With classification, one label is correct and a match check suffices. With open-ended text, the space of valid outputs is huge, so overlap with one reference is a weak proxy and a judge must actually understand the content.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Designing human evaluations and measuring agreement
question: Two annotators reach observed agreement 0.80 on a pairwise study where chance agreement is 0.50. What is Cohen's kappa?

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Classifier guards: Llama Guard and NeMo Guardrails rails
question: You deploy Llama Guard and read P(unsafe) from the first token. Moderators complain that too many harmless prompts are blocked. What is the lowest-effort fix to try first?
options: Raise the threshold on P(unsafe)
Retrain the guard on new data
Lower the threshold on P(unsafe)
Remove the policy categories from the prompt
explain: A higher threshold requires more confidence before flagging, which cuts false positives (at the cost of some misses). Removing categories would break the policy; lowering the threshold makes the problem worse.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Continuous batching: scheduling every iteration
question: Budget 2048 tokens per step, chunked prefill on. 50 requests are decoding when a 6,000-token prompt arrives. What happens over the next few steps?
options: The 50 decodes pause until the 6,000-token prefill finishes in one large step
The prompt is rejected because it exceeds the token budget
Each step runs the 50 decode tokens first and spends the remaining 1,998 tokens on the next chunk of the prompt, so the prefill takes about 4 steps while decoding never stops
The prompt is split across 50 requests, one chunk each
explain: Decodes are scheduled first (1 token each), and the leftover budget goes to prefill chunks: 6,000 / 1,998 is a bit over 3, so 4 steps. Inter-token latency of the 50 stays bounded, and the new request's TTFT grows a little in exchange.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
question: Spot the bug: a scheduler allocates blocks on demand, admits a new request whenever its prompt's blocks are free, and has no preemption code. What eventually happens under heavy load?
options: Running requests need new blocks that are not there, so the step cannot proceed: an out-of-memory failure or a deadlock
Nothing, block allocation can never fail
Throughput drops but every request still finishes
Requests are silently truncated to their prompt length and returned
explain: On-demand allocation without a fallback is exactly the deadlock Orca's reservation avoids: every running request may need one more block at the same moment. You need either worst-case reservation or preemption with swap or recompute.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Constrained decoding: masking logits with a state machine
question: At state 6 the model's probabilities are true 0.15, false 0.34, fa 0.10, and everything else is masked. What is the masked probability of 'false'?
explain: Renormalize over the allowed set: the allowed mass is 0.15 + 0.34 + 0.10 = 0.59, and 0.34 divided by 0.59 gives 0.58. Masking never changes the ratios between legal tokens; it only removes illegal ones.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: From extracted strings to canonical IDs and a bool query
question: A developer moves the location clauses to the top-level bool: `{"bool": {"filter": [title, seniority, skill, salary], "should": [Berlin, remote]}}`. What happens to Fay in Hamburg (not remote, salary 125k)?
options: The profile is returned: with filter clauses present, should defaults to minimum_should_match 0, so location only affects the score
The profile is excluded, because should always requires at least one clause to match
Elasticsearch rejects the query because should cannot be combined with filter
The profile is excluded, because filter clauses are evaluated after should clauses
explain: The docs state the default is 1 only when there are should clauses and no must or filter clauses. Here filter exists, so the default is 0 and the should clauses only add score. Nest the disjunction in its own bool, or set minimum_should_match explicitly.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Calls and tokens per query for each method
question: You change RankGPT's window from w=20, s=10 to w=40, s=20 at k=100, L=100. Why do input tokens fall only from 19,080 to 16,480 although calls fall from 9 to 4?
options: The larger window tokenizes more efficiently
Larger windows truncate passages
The output permutation is shorter
Passages are still read about twice, since s = w/2; only the per-window instruction and query overhead is saved
explain: Input is about 2kL plus C(I+q), where C is the number of windows. Only the C(I+q) term shrinks with fewer windows: 9 x 120 versus 4 x 120. RankGPT's own appendix (Table 12) also found larger windows did not raise nDCG@10 on DL19.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: Budget: 400 ms of model time per query, 100 retrieved candidates. Using the course model, which design fits?
options: Cross-encoder over 100, then a FIRST-style 7B on the top 20
Generated listwise with a 7B model over all 100
Pointwise 7B over all 100 on one GPU
PRP-Sliding-10 with a 7B model
explain: Cross-encoder 56 ms plus one 265 ms FIRST window is about 321 ms. The others: 10.35 s, 2.75 s and about 39.6 s.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Listwise permutation generation with sliding windows
question: RankGPT reranks the BM25 top 100 with w = 20 and s = 10, one pass. The 3rd most relevant passage overall sits at BM25 rank 95. If the model ranks every window perfectly, where does it end up?
options: Rank 3
Somewhere in ranks 81 to 100, because windows only reorder locally
Rank 11, the top of the second window
It is dropped from the list
explain: In every window it enters it is among the top 10 (only 2 passages anywhere beat it), so it is always carried into the next window. The 2 better passages ride up the same way, and the last window (ranks 1 to 20) sorts them exactly: rank 3. A passage outside the overall top w - s = 10 has no such guarantee.

courseTitle: LLM routing and cascades: cheap model or strong model
lessonTitle: Cascades: answer cheaply, score the answer, escalate if unsure
question: You raise the tier-1 threshold of a two-tier cascade from 0.96 to 0.99. What happens?
options: Fewer queries escalate, so cost falls
More queries escalate: cost and mean latency rise, and accuracy usually rises because fewer weak answers are accepted
Nothing changes, since the scorer's outputs are calibrated probabilities
The weak model is skipped for hard queries, so latency falls
explain: A stricter threshold accepts fewer cheap answers, so more queries pay for the strong model and wait for both calls. The weak model still runs on every query; a cascade cannot skip it, only a router can.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: SIFT: keypoints across scale and a 128-number descriptor
question: Why does SIFT compare a candidate with its neighbors in the adjacent DoG scales and not only in its own image?
options: To speed up detection by skipping pixels
To choose a characteristic scale for the keypoint, so the same region is described after a zoom
To compute the 128-d descriptor
To reject points on edges
explain: Being an extremum across scale as well as space picks the blur level where the structure responds most strongly. That scale travels with the keypoint, so after a 2x zoom the detector picks a 2x larger scale and both images describe the same physical region. Edge rejection is the separate Hessian ratio test.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
question: A queue uses only atomic fetch-add and CAS, no mutex. If a producer is preempted between two of its steps, consumers can never dequeue anything past its slot until it resumes. Is the queue lock-free?
options: Yes, because it uses no locks
Yes, because consumers still return (they report empty)
No, because one stalled thread can prevent all other threads from making progress
No, because fetch-add is not a CAS
explain: The definition is about progress: some operation must complete in finite steps no matter which threads stall. Returning "empty" while items are stuck behind a stalled producer is not progress on the queue's contents. Using atomics instead of mutexes is irrelevant to the definition.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Vyukov's bounded MPMC queue: a sequence number per cell
question: Why must the capacity be a power of two in Vyukov's original code?
options: Because CAS only works on power-of-two addresses
So that the cell index is pos & buffer_mask_, a cheap mask that stays consistent as pos grows forever
So that sequence numbers never wrap
Because cache lines are 64 bytes
explain: The constructor asserts buffer_size is a power of two and stores buffer_size - 1 as the mask. Masking only equals pos mod capacity for powers of two. crossbeam lifts the restriction by splitting stamps into an index and a lap instead.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: How accurate is this really, and by which metric
question: A vendor says their parser reaches 0.95 accuracy on your logs. Which single follow-up question is most likely to change your decision?
options: Which programming language is it written in?
Is that per message or per template, and does correct mean grouped correctly or every token identified correctly?
What similarity threshold did you use?
How many datasets did you average over?
explain: Message-level grouping metrics are dominated by frequent templates: 0.95 is reachable by parsing only the 1 percent of templates that carry 95 percent of the volume. Template-level FGA and the token-exact FTA are far stricter, and Drain's FGA falls from about 0.75 to 0.55 when moving from 2,000-line samples to fully annotated million-line logs. The threshold and the language matter much less than knowing what the number counts.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
question: An attacker signs in with a stolen password, approves their own newly registered MFA device, and reads files in a SaaS (software as a service: a hosted web application) app. No program runs on any company laptop. Which source is most likely to show it?
options: Endpoint process creation logs
The identity provider's sign-in and MFA registration logs
Firewall deny records
DNS query logs
explain: Valid-credential intrusions leave little on endpoints or networks. The identity provider records the unusual sign-in and the new device, which is exactly the signal FireEye, a US security company, followed in 2020 (lesson 16).

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Time: clocks, time zones and the order of events
question: Which timestamp should a scheduled rule window on to avoid missing late-arriving events?
options: @timestamp only
event.ingested, or overlapping @timestamp windows with duplicate suppression
The analyst's local clock
The PRI field
explain: Windowing on arrival time guarantees every stored event is searched once. Overlapping windows on event time work too, at the price of deduplication.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Sigma: one rule format, many SIEMs
question: Why does a rule say `category: process_creation, product: windows` instead of naming Sysmon?
options: Sigma cannot read Sysmon
So one rule applies to any Windows process-creation source; processing pipelines map it to Sysmon, 4688 or an EDR feed per environment
Category is required by Splunk
To lower the rule's level
explain: The abstract logsource is what makes rules portable. The environment-specific mapping lives in the pipeline, not in every rule.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Baselines, anomalies and UEBA: how Storm-0558 was caught
question: Which of these is a limit of anomaly detection that Sommer and Paxson identify?
options: It cannot run on network data
It needs Sigma rules
The semantic gap: an alert says something is unusual, not why it is malicious, so analysts must interpret it
It only works on Windows
explain: Unusual is not the same as malicious. Without context the analyst cannot act, which is why anomaly output works best as an investigation lead.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
question: A colleague implements YaRN by scaling queries by 1.2773 for s = 16 but forgets the keys. What is the effect on the logits?
options: Correct: the temperature is defined on queries only
Logits are unchanged because softmax is scale invariant
Logits are scaled by 1.2773 instead of the intended 1.6314
Logits are scaled by 1.6314 squared
explain: YaRN multiplies both rotated q and k (via cos and sin) by sqrt(1/t) = 0.1 ln 16 + 1 = 1.2773, so the dot product is scaled by 1.2773 squared = 1.6314. Scaling only one side gives just 1.2773. Softmax is shift invariant, not scale invariant.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Depth without parameters: what looping a block buys
question: On i-GSM, (1 x 8) scores 73.2%, (8 x 1) scores 73.2% and (1 x 1) scores 24.5%. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Looping only helps because it adds parameters
The task is limited by memorized knowledge, so parameters matter most
The task mainly needs sequential depth; parameters beyond one layer add little here
Looped models are always as good as deep models on every task
explain: The looped model has the parameters of (1 x 1) but matches (8 x 1), so what the extra layers provided was depth, not capacity. That does not generalize to every task: later in the course you will see that knowledge-heavy tasks do need parameters.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Training for any loop count: random depth and truncated backprop
question: Gradients flow only through the last 8 core iterations. Why does the prelude still get trained on every step?
options: It does not; the prelude is frozen after warm-up
Because the coda shares weights with the prelude
Because the no-grad iterations are re-run with gradients at the end of the step
Because e is injected into every iteration, including the last 8, so gradients reach the prelude through each of them
explain: The adapter concatenates s and e at every iteration. During the last k recorded iterations, the loss depends on e through k paths, so the prelude receives gradient from all of them. Only the tied embedding is shared between input and output head, not the prelude layers.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Learned depth per token: Mixture-of-Recursions, Ouro, HRM and TRM
question: TRM's effective depth per supervision step is T x (n + 1) x layers. With T = 3, n = 6 and a 2-layer network, what is it, and how much over 16 supervision steps?
options: 42 per step, 672 in total
36 per step, 576 in total
42 per step, 42 in total because the state is detached
18 per step, 288 in total
explain: 3 x 7 x 2 = 42 layers per supervision step, as in the paper's Table 1, and 42 x 16 = 672 across all steps. Detaching cuts the gradient between steps, not the computation: the answer still benefits from all 672 layers of refinement.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: QLoRA: fine-tuning on top of a 4-bit base model
question: During QLoRA training, which statement about the 4-bit base weights is true?
options: They are updated in 4 bits by a special optimizer
They are converted to BF16 once at load time and kept that way
They are dequantized to BF16 for each matmul, gradients pass through them, but they are never updated
They are skipped in the backward pass, so earlier layers get no gradient
explain: The NF4 weights are the storage format. Each use dequantizes them to BF16 for the forward and backward matmuls, so gradients reach earlier adapters, but no weight gradient or optimizer state is kept for the frozen base.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Unlearning by replacement: Who's Harry Potter and RMU
question: RMU drops Zephyr-7B's WMDP-Bio accuracy from 63.7% to 31.2% while overall MMLU moves from 58.1% to 57.1%. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The hazardous knowledge has been erased from the weights
RMU has no side effects
The model no longer answers the proxy questions, with little general cost but real loss in nearby topics like virology
WMDP-Bio is now harder than random guessing
explain: Multiple-choice accuracy near 25% means the model no longer selects the right answers. The table also shows MMLU virology falling from 52.4% to 25.9%, so related benign knowledge was hit. Whether the knowledge is still in the weights is a separate question that fine-tuning attacks answer (Lesson 5).

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: A safe analysis lab and the analysis workflow
question: Which lab setting most directly lets a sample damage files on your real computer?
options: Taking a snapshot before the run
A shared folder between the VM and the host
Running INetSim on a second VM
Keeping the sample in a ZIP with the password infected
explain: A shared folder is a path from guest to host, so ransomware in the VM can encrypt host files through it. Snapshots, a fake internet and zipped storage all reduce risk.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: The stack in assembly: tracing a compiled function
question: In this unoptimised build, what does `cmp eax, dword ptr [rbp+0x18]` followed by `jl 0x1f` implement?
options: The return statement
The loop condition i < len
Adding buf[i] to sum
Saving the frame pointer
explain: eax holds i, rbp+0x18 holds len. If i < len (signed), jump back to the loop body at 0x1f; otherwise fall through to the return.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Writing and testing YARA rules
question: A colleague's rule has one string, "kernel32.dll" nocase, and its condition is just that string. What is wrong with it?
options: Nothing; it will find malware reliably
nocase is not a valid modifier
Almost every Windows program contains that string, so it will match huge numbers of clean files
Rules must start with uint16(0)
explain: kernel32.dll appears in nearly every PE's import table. A rule needs strings distinctive to the family, ideally combined with cheap structural conditions.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Training a Matryoshka model: one loss per prefix, summed
question: In the toy batch at m = 2, the Matryoshka-style model's loss is about 0.462. Why that value?
options: Two of the three queries score their match and one negative almost equally, giving about ln 2 = 0.693 each; averaged over 3 rows that is 0.462
It is the full-size loss divided by 2 because m = 2
Each row contributes 0.462 because the scale is 20
It is a random number; losses at small prefixes are noise
explain: With two near-equal scores, softmax puts about half its probability on the correct document, and the cross-entropy is -ln(0.5) = 0.693. q1 and q2 each pay that, q3 pays about 0, so the batch mean is 2 x 0.693 / 3 = 0.462.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule
question: p = 8 pipeline stages, m = 32 microbatches, interleaved with v = 4 chunks per device. What is the bubble as a fraction of ideal time?
explain: (p - 1) / (v m) = 7 / (4 x 32) = 7/128 = 5.5%. Without interleaving it would be 7/32 = 21.9%.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Virtual addresses, page tables and the DTB, walked by hand
question: A tool translates kernel address 0x851A6610 but uses the wrong DTB. What happens?
options: It still gets the right answer, because kernel addresses never need translation
The image file becomes corrupted
The CPU in the analysis machine corrects the error
It follows the wrong tree of page tables, so it reads unrelated physical pages or finds entries marked not present
explain: Translation depends entirely on the starting table. With the wrong root every later lookup lands somewhere unrelated; the analysis machine's CPU plays no part in reading an image.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Finding processes: walking the list versus scanning for tags
question: psscan shows two entries for PID 1992 dwm.exe with the same create time and different physical offsets; pslist shows one. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Two different processes share PID 1992
A rootkit cloned dwm.exe
pslist has a bug that drops processes
One is the live object and the other a stale copy left in memory, so there is one process, not a hidden twin
explain: Windows does not run two live processes with the same PID. Identical PIDs and times at different physical offsets point to leftover memory, which scanners find because they ignore whether memory is in use.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Handles, mutexes, sockets and registry hives in memory
question: netscan shows a TCP connection to 203.0.113.50:443 in state CLOSED, owned by a PID that is in psscan but not in pslist, with an exit time. What does this tell you?
options: Nothing: closed connections are always false positives
The analyst's workstation made the connection
The PID is still running and hidden
A process that has since exited made that connection; its objects survived in memory, so hunt the address and investigate the process's history
explain: Scanners recover objects that are no longer in use. An exit time means the process ended normally or was killed; the connection and process are still evidence of what happened.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Timelines from memory: what carries a time, and merging it
question: A thread in explorer.exe was created at 10:42, while explorer itself started at 08:05 and malfind flags the region where the thread starts. What does the thread time add?
options: Nothing; thread times are random
It proves explorer was restarted at 10:42
It dates when the injected code started running, which you can match against other events around 10:42
It is the time the image was acquired
explain: A thread created long after its process began, starting in a flagged region, dates the injection. Look for what happened just before 10:42 on this host and its neighbours.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
question: Under jemalloc, which request wastes the largest fraction of its block?
options: 1,000 bytes
33 bytes
300 bytes
2,048 bytes
explain: 33 bytes rounds to the 48-byte class (16-byte spacing among small classes), wasting 31.25%. The manual's 20% bound holds for all but the smallest classes. 1,000 goes to 1,024 (2.3%), 300 to 320 (6.25%), and 2,048 is exactly a class (0%).

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
question: A colleague says: "Our lock-free queue misbehaves in release builds, so we will ship it compiled with optimizations off." Why does this not make it correct?
options: Debug builds use different atomics
It does: without optimization the compiler emits code in source order and the bug disappears
The CPU can still reorder memory operations, and the compiler still may perform some transformations
Optimization level only affects speed, never ordering
explain: Mara Bos lists this as a myth: disabling optimization does not disable every compiler transformation, and it does nothing about store buffers, pipelining or other CPU reordering. The fix is to use the right orderings.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: On x86-64, which of these Rust operations compiles to a different instruction than its Relaxed version?
options: x.load(SeqCst)
x.load(Acquire)
x.store(1, SeqCst)
x.store(1, Release)
explain: Only the SeqCst store changes: it becomes xchg so that it cannot be delayed past later loads. SeqCst loads stay mov, because the cost is placed on the store side. Mixing the two possible conventions across compilers would break programs, which is why the mapping table recommends the store-side one.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: RCU: publish a new version, free the old after a grace period
question:
Spot the bug:
`rcu_read_lock(); p = rcu_dereference(head.next); rcu_read_unlock(); x = p->data;`
options: rcu_dereference should be rcu_assign_pointer
rcu_read_lock cannot be called on head.next
There is no bug because readers never block
p->data is read after rcu_read_unlock, so a grace period may have ended and p may be freed
explain: Once the critical section ends, the reader no longer delays grace periods, so an updater's synchronize_rcu() can return and kfree(p). The kernel documentation shows exactly this pattern marked BUG. Read p->data before rcu_read_unlock(), or take a reference count to keep it longer.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: The call stack: frames, return addresses and saved frame pointers
question: Which value does the CPU use to decide where to continue after `ret`?
options: The saved frame pointer
The address of main, which it remembers in a hidden register
The 8 bytes in the return-address slot of the current frame
The value of buf
explain: ret pops the top slot of the frame into rip. The CPU does not check where that value came from. If those 8 bytes changed, the return goes somewhere else.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Off-by-one: a single byte too far
question: Why can overwriting only the lowest byte of a saved frame pointer still change where a program goes?
options: The frame pointer is restored into rbp and later used to find the caller's saved return address, which now comes from attacker-influenced memory
It makes the CPU reset
It changes the instruction pointer immediately
It cannot; one byte is always harmless
explain: The corrupted saved frame pointer becomes the caller's rbp. When the caller returns, it reads its saved values relative to that rbp, which now points into the buffer. Control is redirected one return later.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Finding memory bugs: warnings, sanitizers, Valgrind and fuzzing
question: A team ships a C library that parses image files from the internet. Which single practice would most likely have caught the Stagefright-style size bugs before release?
options: Code comments explaining each size
Increasing all buffer sizes by 50 percent
Running the parser under a debugger once
Coverage-guided fuzzing of the parser built with AddressSanitizer
explain: Fuzzing generates exactly the strange sizes and lengths that trigger overflow and wraparound bugs, and ASan turns each silent overflow into a precise report. Comments and one debugger run do not explore inputs; bigger buffers only move the boundary.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
question: In a P = 16, K = 4 batch with batch hard mining, how many triplet terms contribute to the loss?
explain: Batch hard produces one triplet per anchor, and every image in the batch is an anchor: P x K = 64 terms. The last option is the batch all count PK(PK - K)(K - 1).

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: DoNotOptimize, loop hoisting and who owns the loop
question: Why does JMH discourage writing your own repeat loop inside a @Benchmark method?
options: Loops in Java cannot be JIT compiled
JMH cannot count loop iterations, so the result is reported per call instead of per operation
Loops prevent the method from being inlined into the harness
The optimizer can unroll the loop and hoist or merge the repeated operation, so cost per operation shrinks with the repeat count
explain: JMHSample_11_Loops shows the perceived per-operation cost falling as the repeat count grows, to about 1/20 ns per addition, because the loop is unrolled and pipelined and the operation is hoisted. @OperationsPerInvocation does the division correctly; the measured code is what is wrong.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Fully async RL: busy engines, paid for in staleness
question: In a fully async run, queue_size sits at the buffer capacity every step and buffer_max_staleness keeps rising. What is the most direct fix?
options: Add rollout GPUs, because generation is the bottleneck
Give training more capacity (or lower generation concurrency), because the trainer cannot drain the buffer fast enough
Switch submission granularity from sample to group
Raise --async-data-buffer-capacity-factor so more groups fit
explain: A full buffer means rollout produces faster than training consumes. The docs suggest more training GPUs, lower concurrency, or latency-oriented SGLang settings. A bigger buffer only lets groups grow staler, and more rollout GPUs make the imbalance worse.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Beyond GRPO: distillation, exact alignment and a 744B run
question: You want to distill a large teacher with a different tokenizer into your student using --opd-type sglang. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; the SGLang teacher retokenizes the student's text
The teacher must share the student's tokenizer, because it scores the student's token IDs
Only the megatron mode allows different architectures
The top-K variant is required for different tokenizers
explain: In SGLang mode the teacher scores the student's sampled token IDs directly, so the IDs must mean the same tokens to both models. A different architecture is fine; a different tokenizer is not. Megatron mode requires the same architecture.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Deploying learned policies: inference budgets, drift and guardrails
question: Which statement about learned indexes, LRB and Decima is correct?
options: All three need the model to be correct to return correct results
None of them needs retraining once deployed
In all three, the model chooses among options the system already guarantees are valid, so mistakes cost performance rather than correctness
All three use deep neural networks at decision time
explain: The index searches a verified window (or a B-tree leaf), LRB evicts some cached object, and Decima only schedules runnable stages. Model quality changes speed or miss ratio. LRB uses GBMs and the index uses mostly linear leaves, and both indexes and caches need retraining as data changes.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Dynamic analysis: a test device, a proxy and the app's own files
question: You install Burp's CA certificate in the user store of a lab phone and set the Wi-Fi proxy. A browser's traffic appears in Burp, but the shopping app (release build, targets API 34, no network security config) shows only failed handshakes. What does this tell you?
options: The app is pinning certificates, which is a vulnerability
Burp is misconfigured, because the browser would fail too
The app is using the platform default for apps targeting Android 7.0 and later: it trusts only system CAs, which is correct behaviour
The app does not use HTTPS
explain: Since API level 24, apps trust only the system store unless their network security config says otherwise; with no config they use that safe default. The browser trusts user CAs, so it works. Failed handshakes show TLS is in use and validated. Use a debug build or a system-store CA on a rooted lab device.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Deep links: custom schemes, App Links and Universal Links
question: Why does RFC 8252 forbid using an in-app WebView for the OAuth login page?
options: WebViews cannot display HTTPS pages
WebViews do not support JavaScript
The app hosting the WebView can read what the user types and the cookies, so a malicious or compromised app could capture the user's credentials for the identity provider
Identity providers block WebView user agents by law
explain: In an embedded user-agent the host app controls the page and can inspect it, which defeats the point of OAuth (the app should never see the password). The system browser or an in-app browser tab keeps the identity provider's page out of the app's reach.

courseTitle: Mobile app security testing: OWASP MASVS and MASTG
lessonTitle: Resilience and attestation: what an app can prove, and what it cannot
question: In the assertion model, why must the server check that the counter increases, when the signature already proves the request came from the attested key?
options: Because signatures can be forged when the counter is low
Because the counter encrypts the request
Because Apple requires a counter on every HTTP request
Because a captured, validly signed request could otherwise be replayed as-is; the counter and the one-time challenge make each assertion usable once
explain: A signature says who signed, not how many times the bytes may be used. Our run shows the replay passing the signature check but failing the counter check. Apple's server-side steps include both the counter comparison and matching the one-time challenge.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
question: Which property of matrix multiplication makes absorbing $W^{UK}$ into the query legal?
options: Commutativity: $AB = BA$
Associativity: $(AB)C = A(BC)$, so the up-projection can be grouped with the query instead of the latent
Distributivity over the softmax
Invertibility of $W^{UK}$
explain: Only regrouping is needed. Matrix products are not commutative in general, and $W^{UK}$ is not square (it maps 512 to 128 x 128), so it is not invertible. Lesson 4 shows how RoPE breaks this regrouping.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, FP8 cache
question: FlashMLA's FP8 cache for DeepSeek-V3.2 quantizes the 512 latent values but keeps the 64 RoPE values in BF16. Which statement is right?
options: The RoPE part must be BF16 because FP8 cannot represent rotations
The README gives accuracy as the reason, and it costs little: 128 of the 656 bytes
The RoPE part is kept in BF16 because it is shared by all heads and so is never read
FP8 with scale stores the whole row, RoPE included, in E4M3
explain: The README states the RoPE part "is not quantized for accuracy". Rotation math works on any number format, and the RoPE key is read for every score. Keeping it in BF16 adds 64 bytes per row compared with quantizing it too.

courseTitle: Serving many LoRA adapters on one base model
lessonTitle: Batching different adapters: Punica's SGMV kernel
question: A batch of 64 decode rows is spread across 64 different adapters. According to Punica's roofline analysis, what limits the SGMV kernel?
options: Tensor Core throughput, because there are 64 matmuls
Memory bandwidth, because each row reads its own adapter weights and does little math per byte
PCIe bandwidth (the CPU-to-GPU bus), because adapters are always loaded from the CPU
Nothing: the cost is identical to one shared adapter
explain: With n = s_n the I/O term n h_i h_o grows with the batch, so arithmetic intensity stays about 0.94 FLOPs per byte, firmly bandwidth bound. Measured latency rose from 37 to 116 microseconds, versus 37 to 40 for a single shared adapter.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: You configure LlamaIndex `QueryFusionRetriever(num_queries=4, ...)` with one retriever. How many LLM-generated queries and how many searches does one call make?
options: 4 generated, 4 searches
4 generated, 5 searches
3 generated, 4 searches
1 generated, 4 searches
explain: num_queries counts the original. The prompt asks the LLM for num_queries - 1 = 3 queries, and the original plus those 3 are each searched once per retriever: 4 searches. Setting num_queries=1 disables generation.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
question: The LLM sometimes returns phrasings that shift the question to a neighboring topic. Which change most directly limits the damage?
options: Raise N so the drifted phrasing is outvoted
Keep the original query in the set and inspect or filter generated queries that look off-topic
Replace RRF with an unranked union
Drop the original query to avoid bias
explain: The original query cannot drift and anchors fusion. Filtering clearly off-topic rewrites (or constraining the prompt) removes the junk list. Raising N adds cost and may add more drift; a union passes drifted results straight through.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: RankGPT reranks M = 100 passages with w = 20 and s = 10. You switch to w = 20, s = 5 to give passages more chances to move. How many LLM calls does one pass now make?
explain: ceil((100 - 20) / 5) + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17 calls, reading 17 x 20 = 340 passages. Smaller steps mean more overlap and almost double the cost of s = 10. The guaranteed-correct top also grows, from w - s = 10 to 15.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Why lookahead helps, and where it does not
question: You have a 7B code model pretrained with 4-token prediction and want the best model for a new coding task. Based on Gloeckle et al.'s CodeContests fine-tuning, what should you try first?
options: Fine-tune with the 4-token loss, since the heads are already trained
Fine-tune a next-token-pretrained model with a 4-token loss instead
Skip fine-tuning; MTP models cannot be fine-tuned
Fine-tune with plain next-token loss after dropping the extra heads
explain: Both ways of fine-tuning the 4-token model beat the next-token baseline, and next-token fine-tuning on top of 4-token pretraining was best overall. Adding a 4-token loss to an already trained next-token model (Llama 2, Table S6) gave no significant gain.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
question: An MTP model with one extra draft has acceptance rate 0.9. Under the simplified independence model, about how many tokens does each forward pass yield, and why is the measured speedup lower?
options: 1.9 tokens; verification passes cost a little more than plain decode steps
2.0 tokens; the draft is always accepted at greedy temperature
1.81 tokens, because 0.9 squared is 0.81
1.9 tokens; the speedup is lower because outputs differ from greedy decoding
explain: Expected tokens = 1 + a = 1.9. The wall-clock gain is smaller because each verifying pass processes extra positions and runs the drafter. Output does not differ: greedy verification reproduces greedy decoding exactly. DeepSeek-V3 reports 85% to 90% acceptance and 1.8x tokens per second.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Why orthogonalize: steepest descent under the spectral norm
question: A weight has 1024 outputs and 4096 inputs. Using the RMS-to-RMS derivation, what factor multiplies $UV^\top$, and what does the reference Muon code use?
options: Derived 0.5, code 1
Derived 2, code 2
Derived 0.5, code 0.5
Derived 1, code 2
explain: The derived factor is $\sqrt{\text{fan-out}/\text{fan-in}} = \sqrt{1024/4096} = 0.5$. The code uses $\sqrt{\max(1, 1024/4096)} = 1$ because it clamps at 1. They agree only for tall matrices.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon in a real training stack: parameter groups, sharding and code
question: With ZeRO-1, why does Distributed Muon need an extra collective that distributed AdamW does not?
options: Newton-Schulz needs the full momentum matrix, but each rank only holds a shard of it
Muon's momentum is stored in fp64 and must be broadcast
Muon recomputes gradients on every rank
Muon needs the Hessian, which is sharded across ranks
explain: AdamW's update is elementwise, so a rank can update its shard alone. Orthogonalization mixes all entries of the matrix, so Moonlight adds a bf16 DP gather of the momentum, runs Newton-Schulz on the full matrix and keeps only the local slice.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Why 'maximal': kernel, mean-field and feature-learning limits
